utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everybody. Thank you for allowing me to address you. The cause for my request was my concern that perhaps here there are three notions of the same indictment in view of the fact that the Trial Chamber often objects to my line of questioning. The way I understand the indictment and the way the Prosecution stated that I have not done anything, I believe that the focus of the indictment is the fact that I wanted to expel Muslims and Croats from the territory that the Serbs thought that they had a right to. The right to territory is not a crime. A crime is the allegation that I wanted those territories to be ethnically clean and that's why I started a war, and in order to do that I put conditions in place for the war to happen and for the war to serve the purpose of that goal. If that, indeed, is the case, then I don't have to dwell upon individual murders or killings because that would be part of a civil war. I did not have any contacts with that part of the state until September. So what remains is who wanted the war and who had goals? I claim that it was the Muslims' goal to expel us from that same territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Robinson foreshadowed this -- well, what turns out to be a submission earlier and explained that Dr. Karadzic wanted to address a relevance issue raised by the Court. Now what we're seeing is submissions, commentary, testimony. It's -- this is not an appropriate submission. If Dr. Karadzic wants to raise a response to a relevance objection, in this case one -- I don't know if it's an objection or a comment noted by the Court is what I understood is the point of Dr. Karadzic's seeking some time to address the Court that's one matter, but to start testifying about his actions, his intentions, and to make an argument in general is neither an appropriate use of court time nor -- and appropriate submission to make at this point in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can he not explain his case, about his case, in addressing the relevance, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I understand those two -- those two overlap, clearly, and to make a point about relevance, he's going to touch on those issues, but I noted he's making factual submissions about both the evidence and also offering testimony about his own state of mind, and those things need to be kept separate from and -- and only arise until the appropriate context in the case. That's -- that's my point. If -- here's one: "I did not have any contacts with that part of the state until September," is his claim. That's testimony or comment or something else. That has no place in -- in what should be a pointed submission, a succinct submission, about relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that -- I take it to mean his way of defence strategy, but I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tieger, one must remember that Dr. Karadzic is acting not only as defendant but as advocate, but if he were to say those things as an advocate in response to a question as to the relevance of the advocate's line of cross-examination, it would be put in pretty much the same way. He uses the word -- the personal pronoun simply because he's occupying two positions rather than saying, "my client -- my client's case is," he's saying, "My case is." I can understand your objection if the defendant was making a legal submission, but he's not. He is setting out his stall as to what his factual position is that he sees he has to defend as a matter of mixed fact and law. Am I right about that, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Excellency, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Chamber is unanimous in this point. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I want to avoid a situation in which I would be on the wrong track, and I also want to avoid any misunderstandings with the Trial Chamber and that may be due to my amateurism, and if my strategic orientation in defence is also wrong, then I am in great difficulty. So if my understanding is what it is, then I have to prove who wanted the war in the first place and how the war happened. These are the problems that I see from the place of head of state and the head of army who handed over his tactical command to somebody else. I can't be responsible or should I say my client cannot be responsible for people killing each other. They have been killing each other always, but I can be responsible -- respond to the allegations that I needed the war in order to achieve my criminal goal. I have to prove differently, and I can prove that that was not the case, if I understood the indictment properly and if I understood the role of the Defence in this case properly. Thank you very much. Unfortunately, the interpretation is not good. I am saying that people have been killing each other, especially in the Balkans, especially in Bosnia, since the time when these two religions have existed and this is the position of a civilian head of state and head of army who is not in tactical command. And, thirdly, I am expressing the views of my defendant of the goals and the means to achieve those goals and these are different than are alleged in the statement, and I will not be able to prove that if I don't clarify that with the Prosecution witnesses. I will have my Defence case later, but now they are presenting their case, and I have to challenge that. First of all, I have to know whether I'm right in -- in interpreting the indictment, whether I understand the indictment and the charges against me properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, we're not going to explain what the Prosecution indictment is. I think it's self-evident and you have Mr. Robinson to assist you as to any legal difficulties you may have to address as to that, and I don't think you have to take the rather schizophrenic view of actually dividing yourself into defendant and lawyer in the -- in your language. We understand both. I was simply making a point. Yes, of course, you have to set out your case, and it's entirely a matter for you. What I would simply urge is what the Chamber has urged upon before you before, that to try and deal with matters as a matter of law where you can and remember that it's you that's the subject of the indictment, not Serbia, nor the Serbian people. So you can perhaps focus your case more acutely on the indictment rather than the broader historical perspective. I speak for myself, but I'm sure I speak for my colleagues. We're not trying to restricting you. We're just trying to make it more focused or everybody's benefit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. How are you, sir, today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you very much. I'm very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I hope that you will appreciate my effort to narrow down my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that the strategic orientation towards the left bank of the Sana was not only yours but also the people from Bihac and you mentioned that the strategic plans were devised by those who were sitting in Sarajevo at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was an estimate of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the first Cutileiro's map envisaged for this to be a canton without any contacts with Cazin Krajina? Before the war nobody was worried for the continuity of the territory. I accepted that. And let me continue the second Cutileiro's map gave a lot of Prijedor and Sanski Most to the Cazin Krajina and I also accepted that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Vance-Owen's plan reached as far as the left bank of the Sana? You will remember the triangle. And there was a mine there, Ljubija, Sanski Most, and a lot of Sanski Most was supposed to be given to the Cazin Krajina, and I remember that as well.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- and I accepted that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember. And then, surprise, how it occurred to you that the Prijedor was strategically important for the Serbs. Something to that effect can be found in the description of events. I would like to know whether you are familiar with the description of events that is enclosed with the indictment and with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we're talking about two different processes. One process entailed political negotiations aimed at reaching compromises, and the second situation deals with the potential conflict. I spoke about the strategic importance of Prijedor and why Prijedor experienced what it did, why its fate was, in a way, bad. It had three -- 3.500 casualties. Only Srebrenica had more casualties than Prijedor. I have some ideas why that happened, and one of the reasons why that happened in my view is position of Prijedor, which is only about 55 kilometres or 30 miles from Banja Luka, and there were a lot of Bosniaks there residing in the Sana valley. The second reason is the fact that Prijedor was before that a town with a Serb majority. According to the 1981 census, there were 43 per cent Serbs and 38 per cent Bosniak, and in 1991, that was reversed, 44 per cent Bosniak and 45 per cent Serbs. And the third thing that was the cause of Prijedor's fate was the fact that although the SDA and all the other places where Serbs constituted a minority of maybe 5 or 6 per cent, the SDS still managed to win the elections save in Prijedor, and, Mr. Karadzic, you wanted to reconcile two different streams within your own people. One stream was a Partisan stream as it were and the other was Chetnik and the situation was the same in Prijedor. The first president, Mr. Srdjo Srdic was an urban Serb, was a member of the so-called Partisan stream. In the pre-election campaign, Stojan Vracar together with Marko Pavic and Sejmenovic were on the list and they split the number of votes for the Council of Municipalities. And then when Marko Pavic and Mevludin Sejmenovic together embarked on the campaign, it was almost certain that Marko Pavic would win, but he didn't because he did not manage to attract the votes of the Orthodox Serbs, i.e., the Chetnik stream. Those people actually vote for Mevludin Sejmenovic rather than Marko Pavic who had belonged to the Communist stream?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It would be very nice to go and listen to you but I don't have time. Very well, do you remember that even after the takeover and even after the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May the Serb side wanted you to have your own municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke a lot about that in the Stakic trial. One stream within the party, indeed, believed that something like that was realistic and possible. I personally encouraged them to follow that line of negotiations if they thought that was indeed realistic. I personally believed that the entire process that was taking place in Prijedor was a process that was well designed and that would have an identical ultimate outcome irrespective of what moves we made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we agree that the Serbs accepted a Muslim canton in the Sana valley, and if they accepted for a lot of the Cazin Krajina to belong to the Muslims and to have a separate municipality within a town like Sarajevo has ten municipalities, would you not agree that it was not our interest for Muslims to disappear from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I thought long and hard about that, and I analysed why Prijedor fared as it did. Sadikovic, Esad, I don't know if the name means anything to you. He was a physician, his wife was Serb, and he spent working with Medecins sans Frontieres working many countries. He was a cosmopolitan. He was -- he was a friend with many Serbs, and he was killed in Omarska. How come that Mr. Sikora who was very beloved by the Serbs he was also killed. Allow me to finish. Two sentences, Mr. Karadzic. The reason for that is the Prijedor's Partisans' past. It had to be shown to people on the examples of Dr. Sadikovic and Mr. Sikora who was a Czech, he was not the member of any party that they were enemies of the Serbs and they should serve to create a gap between the traditionally good relationships -- relations between the Serbs and the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you said it yourself that I did everything in my power for the Partisan Chetniks to reconcile. So how come that the Chetnik stream was so strong there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what you could do on your part was to have one line advocated by Srdic and Kupresanin and you could strike some deals because they were in favour of peaceful political options and they could have stayed in power. However, after the elections, the whole thing was radicalised when Stakic surged to power and he was a radical. Brdjanin was also another radical person. He replaced Kupresanin who was a much more moderate person. All those were signals to us that in that area the room for political solutions were -- was being decreased.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look at 1D187. I will go through some documents as fast as I can, and I will take them according to a chronology. This document was issued on the 13th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will see here that the federal administration for moral guidance describes the events in Prijedor -- or, rather, in that area, not only in Prijedor. Could you please look at the part where it says: [As read] "There are no signs of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina calming down with armed conflicts, chaos, anarchy, terror, and reprisals continuing. The deterioration of the situation is particularly marked in the valleys of the Neretva and Drina Rivers and tensions are also marked in Prijedor, Sanski Most, Stolac, and some other towns." And then the document also says: [As read] "Muslim and Croatian extremists continue to pursue a policy of terror and reprisal against Serbian citizens, maltreating, harassing, and provoking the members of the JNA and their families thus putting pressure on them to leave all with the blessing of the rump BH government and Presidency ...," and so on and so forth. It says here: [As read] "Alija Izetbegovic is undoubtedly making a grave mistake by constantly stressing that external aggression has been carried out and mentioning only Serbia as the external factor in the SDS as the internal one. Objectively speaking, this does not help stem the rise of the Muslim and Croatian hatred against the Serbs and the army ..." Can we go to the following page please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's insufferable for the interpreters. We all can read. Even the witness can read it. Why don't you just put your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Mesud Hasotic was, and is it true he was a Muslim, a Muslim who spent in the ranks of the Serb army a long time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know who Colonel Mesud Hasotic is and I know by his name is that he is a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All you did was read out this document and ask about the author. What's the question to the witness -- for the witness with respect to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Mujadzic, that the army had this type of assessment of the event as early as the 13th of April for the entire Bosnia and it's said that it was even worse in the Neretva and Drina valleys whereas for Prijedor it says that the tensions were rising.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this report was drafted by Mr. Hasotic and on what basis, but I do know that usually this type of report is compiled based on the information that comes from the ground. Now, the question is what the source of this information for this report of Mr. Hasotic's was. Obviously the source was one-sided and it was an exclusively army source, and obviously he did not take into account any information from the other side that would not quite be in sync with what he put in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, but would you agree with me and can we have the first page please that Izetbegovic, as it says here, similarly like Tudjman -- could we have the first page, please, but a slightly in a more -- in a weaker variant is accusing them and that's why -- okay, so adhering to a slightly mild letter variant of the principle Tudjman used, accuses the JNA of acting strangely because it fails to take the side of those in Bosnia who are allegedly defending themselves. Now, do you know, Mr. Witness, that at this time in April Mr. Izetbegovic was accusing the JNA of this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason for criticising the JNA was something that many other people outside of the SDA also found valid. One of those thesis was also publicly voiced in parliament, and I do believe that you recall those discussions. From the very first day of the elections of the 1990 you remember the tax that was extended, the tax of 3 per cent that was to go -- to be allocated to the army, and already at that time the Bosniak members of parliament were not prepared to extend this tax because the army was already taking sides, and it was becoming clear what their position was, that it was becoming increasingly less Yugoslav and increasingly more Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I'm not asking you about the reasons. What I'm asking you was whether you knew that Mr. Izetbegovic took this position.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1836, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D4499.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know Mr. Zeljaja. Here we have a document that he drafted. The document is dated the 15th of April, 1992, and he speaks about developments in the garrison and perhaps we can read portions of it. I hope that we have a translation. No. I've just been told there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in on the document. My apologies. I can't really see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have it blown up, please. Thank you. Can we now scroll the page up a bit. I think that yesterday we agreed, but if not, we can do that today, that this garrison in Prijedor was the base garrison for two brigades, the 5th Kozara Brigade and the 343rd Motorised Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you see here that he talks about the threats of nationalist and chauvinist behaviour, and then under paragraph 3 he says that care should be taken to keep the JNA members outside of the inter-party strifes, and then it says that there is a threat that there may be some attacks on various military installations in Prijedor and Kozarac and so on -- on Kozara and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And here under 6 and on it says that without specific orders, no one is to issue any weapons of the TO and that members of the JNA have to protect the citizens of all ethnicities from any threats against paramilitary units and so on and so forth. Now, when after the 30th of April there was a takeover of power in the area, do you remember that the JNA at that time was the main negotiator and that they were very angry and that they addressed in the same breath, as it were, both the SDA and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that, Mr. Karadzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the SDS Municipal Board on the 23rd of April adopted one of these conclusions, and I will quote it. It says that they want Zeljaja to declare himself, whether he was prepared to defend Serbs or to invite his soldiers to leave the JNA and to surrender their arms.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything of that document, but we never issued such ultimatums to Mr. Zeljaja or to the Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a remark about Mr. Zeljaja. Mr. Karadzic is talking about the 15th of April, 1992, when Major Zeljaja provided this assessment. Now, a mere month later, on the 16th of May exactly, Mr. Zeljaja stated that he was a commander of the Serb army. In other words, just a month later, he suddenly transformed and became a commander of the Republika Srpska Army, and this is really -- he finally came out, as it were, and showed his real face, and we had considered that to be the case already earlier. We had the sense that that's what would happen. Now, he -- in the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his last words, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Just a second. The interpreters didn't hear your last word, Mr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will say that Mr. Zeljaja, after the so-called liberation of Kozarac, renamed Kozarac to Radmilovo. Although this area had a 95 per cent Bosniak population and yet, he chose to give it a new place name that was purely Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark for identification this document pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1837, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Your last words were not interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can't exactly recall what I said, but, yes, I see. Do you agree that on the 15th of April the agreement on the withdrawal of the JNA had not been reached whereas on the 16th of May, that was the case, and the JNA did withdraw. On the 12th of May we took this decision that we would have our own army.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear, Mr. Karadzic. I -- I can agree with that, but we are talking here about the essence, the substantive matters, not the formal aspects. The fact that the JNA de facto was a Serb army, although de jure it was still officially the Yugoslav People's Army, but in fact it was the Serb army already, and soon after that that became very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now see 65 ter 00485. This is a document dated the 1st of May from the command of the 5th Corps. This is still the JNA. The 1st of May, 1992. Would you please take a look at the very first sentence: [As read] "The enemy has indulged in provocative fire from the area of Lipik," in other words from Croatia. And then in the next sentence it says, "In the general area of Bosnian Krajina several developments are making the situation more complex. After the SDA's takeover in Prijedor the situation in general is calm. During the night a killing occurred at a check-point in Prijedor and the Muslim organisation sealed off the village of Kozarac, preventing access to it. In the past few days, HOS members have been fortifying positions on the right bank of the Vrbas River and so on in Donji Vakuf." Now, do you recall that on the 1st of May a Serb policeman, reserve policeman, was killed he was shot in the back and on the 2nd of May his relative, to avenge him, killed four Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that event very clearly, Mr. Karadzic, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well, but you can see what the JNA's assessment of the situation at this time was still. Is it correct that there was a check-point at -- on the approaches to Kozarac at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's correct. There were check-points all over the place, but there is no mention made here that four Bosniaks were killed in the village of Brezicani after this putsch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid these were the same four people who were killed to avenge the relative and that was the reason to introduce a curfew; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. Karadzic, but at the time and if we've talking about the same event, there had not been any killing of a Serb. Rather, members of the Territorial Defence who had Chetnik insignia killed the president of the SDA of the local board in Brezicani and three other citizens of Muslim or Bosniak ethnicity for no reason at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we do have some newspaper reports on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1838.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you can we now have 65 ter 5455, please. 5455.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is addressed to the command of the 2nd Military District dated the 17th of May. In other words we see that this is still the JNA, but it is already well known that we were going to establish our own army, and we don't have to look at the whole thing but it mentions Croatia, Pakrac, Travnik, Dobratic, the HOS has some 400 or 500 armed men but not active and then it goes on to say in the third paragraph in the general area of Prijedor, there were three detachments established of -- of Green Berets, and this would actually be consistent with what you mentioned earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were not Green Berets, they were members of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1839, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 65 ter 17879, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This document is dated the 16th of May, also addressed to the 5th Corps command, where it is reported to them that the enemy's attempting to capture some facility in Vlasic. Now, this is in Central Bosnia, isn't it? Between Kotor Varos and Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you see here that an order is issued to the effect that all measures are to be taken to defend all nodal communication centres and other isolated communication features in the zone of responsibility, and this is addressed to the command of the Prijedor region and to the command of the 122nd Light Infantry Brigade. In other words, the JNA is still considering these facilities their own and they use them for communications; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what we can infer from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1840, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and now can we look at 65 ter 17761.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of May, this is a report by Drljaca who writes to his boss in Banja Luka. In Ljubija and Donje Ljubija; a platoon armed with infantry weapons in Rizvanovici, Hambarine and Biscani; a company armed with infantry weapons in Carakovo; a platoon with infantry weapons in Kozarac and Kozarusa; a company armed with infantry weapons. Do you see that on the 18th of May there was information about the -- these forces in the suburbs of Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, there was never any dispute about that. Those were members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also stated that on the 13th of April, the Serbs took the central part of the city with all the institutions such as radio, the Ministry of the Interior, and so on and so forth, and you also stated that the Serb suburbs were freed. They were not taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. If you are referring to the putsch, i.e., the illegal takeover of power in Prijedor by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted as Exhibit D1841. Mr. Karadzic, your time is up, and I would allow you to put your last question. Just a second. We will mark.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have at least another 15 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification pending translation. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. You have 15 minutes more, Mr. Karadzic, in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, you said a great many things that seem to be discrepant in your statements. Who's this lady in parliament who told you in parliament that I had said that we have the JNA, you have nothing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a lady, it was Mr. Kerovic [phoen] who was from Lopari, MP from Lopari. There was this discussion and you know that very often during breaks MPs chat in the hallway and Mr. Kerovic, you probably remember him, he's from Lopari, he said that to me. He said, "What do you Bosniaks want? We have the JNA, and what have you got? Nothing, you Bosniaks."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in the 92 ter document this number plus 84 you say she said. She said.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That must have been a mistake in translation. What I meant was Mr. Kerovic, a member of parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, is it correct that you had a war Crisis Staff already in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of us ever having a war Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4672. Could we have that, please. It seems it's not -- we'll wait. We'll wait until it's upload order we'll show it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know that both the Muslim and the Serb sides accused you, accused you as the main extremist, as the person who was guilty as far as everything that happened in Prijedor was concerned? Both the Muslim side and the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Mr. Karadzic, the Bosniak side accused me of having co-operated with the Serbs and that I had not armed the people sufficiently and that I was not sufficiently aggressive and belligerent whereas the Serb accusations were the exact opposite. So I had accusations levelled at me from both sides that were completely opposite. What I tried to do throughout was to avoid a conflict altogether, and that is how I ended up being accused by both sides, the Bosniak side for having co-operated with the Serbs and not having done enough to have the Bosniaks defended from the Serb side and then the other way round from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is true. You were accused of having collaborated with the Chetniks. However, Fikret Kadiric said that you were the chief warmonger in Prijedor. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of any such statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at 1D0251. Were court proceedings instituted against you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now we're going to see this. This is an entire case file from the Military Court in Banja Luka. You are aware the fact that indictment was withdrawn at some point after the war in 1990-something.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. No, this is not it. This is a different document. No, no. This is some agreement. 1D02951. I'm going to read this out to you. Criminal report against Mirsad Mujadzic and your brother.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot keep up with all the names being read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Teofik, Esref, your uncle; right? It's 16 persons accused that we have here. Just a moment, please. Let's see which page is this. 627 is the ERN number. Those are the last three digits, rather. Armed rebellion, in October, 627 and then 629. Let us see why.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was this a question addressed to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. Let us see what they accused you of: That in October 1991, you established a Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor consisting of Muslims only and then you were preparing for war, you were arming, and so on and so forth. At any rate, they point out that it is you. Then, in order to have an ethnic balance of the employed in the SJB --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this page, the one that I asked for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it page 3 and 4 in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see. P0056627 is the ERN number. 5667. Those are the last digits. This is on -- this is a decision on staying the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know. I'm not aware of proceedings being instituted or being stayed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 627. So we have to go back. 627.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got a copy of the B/C/S that perhaps it might assist the witness if the registrar's having trouble with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is what we have before us not that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Karadzic was asking for specific pages, and I just thought it might quicken proceedings if the witness had a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just make a brief comment with regard to this comment -- this document and similar documents, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can give us your comments while we're looking for this, but this is a very voluminous case file against you, against you. Sixteen of you from Prijedor. It has to do with a great many things that were done against peace and against the citizens of Prijedor and against the army. It seems that not all of it has been uploaded. Quite simply, this seems to be one blow after the other. Nothing. Then I have to give up on this document altogether. I'll show it some other time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I -- may I just give a brief comment with regard to this document and similar documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Accusations like this coming from the SDS and these documents are entitled "Monster doctor," it has to do with Dr. Sikora, who was a Catholic, a Czech by origin. He was accused of prepared measures of making Serb children sterile, carrying out abortions and so on. This man was a great friend of the Serb people and he was very well liked among the Serb people. This is just an example of this kind of thing. Two messages are being sent out, one to the Serbs, the Serbs in the city of Prijedor, saying see what the Muslims and Croats are preparing, which is aimed against you, although this was not supported by any kind of facts. Secondly, the idea was to create a rift between Serbs and Muslims and Bosniaks. These good relations were traditionally maintained in the area. It is a well-known thing that the Prijedor Bosniaks protected the Serbs in Prijedor many times and that is what they wanted to get rid of. That is what your party in Prijedor did very well, Mr. Karadzic, and I think that that's what you were aiming for when you appointed Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I did not engage in elections at local level, and Stakic comes from a Partisan family. That is what was pointed out to you in the cross-examination in Brdjanin and Stakic. However, this has to do with a Military Court and the SDS had no influence over the Military Court whatsoever. I have to call up yet another document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need three more documents of Muslim provenance and then I'll be done. 1D4672.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that now uploaded?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be uploaded. Yes, I think. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. This is information of the state security where it says here the war Crisis Staff. The date is the 6th of July, and it says Muslim extremists Mujadzic, Mirsad, Camil Pezo and so on on the 23rd of September, 1991, they said that the situation in Prijedor was extraordinary and that they would be working under war conditions, and they formed a war Crisis Staff consisting of three members, Mujadzic, Pezo and Krkic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, whose information is this? I see the date is 1995. Is that the date when this was written up?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the date, and it has to do with what happened in 1991. This is security information about the activities of Dr. Mirsad Mujadzic and other Muslim extremists in Prijedor. This is the secret service, the secret police. You can see that this is strictly confidential.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we never had a war Crisis Staff. We had a Crisis Staff but not a war Crisis Staff. Obviously, this information is inadequate and it was written post festum, four years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If Your Honour would just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, under the rules this would be admitted and it's a matter of weight. The witness has disputed the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the position taken by the Prosecution, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're trying abide by the Court's guidance. I mean we're not trying to override it in this case. The point was we don't dispute the -- we have no basis for disputing the authenticity. We understand that this falls into a slightly different category particularly in light of the fact that the witness has disputed it. We're trying to avoid unnecessary wrangles, but our point was not to -- we're trying to find the right balance between the Court's previous determinations about what's admissible and we're only citing the factors that bear on that consideration. If the Court has concerns about the utility of this document or the weight to be given this -- such a document in light of the length of time that transpired between the events at issue and when this was put together, the nature of the agency which put it together and -- and the purposes for which it was assembled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just put it simply. You're objecting, is it? I asked Ms. Sutherland her position, and I understood her to say that with the caveat given by the witness, she's not objecting to the admission, but -- excuse me. Do you object?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Our position is that this has such little weight to lend the Chamber that we don't think it is of value in these circumstances; correct. But we're -- because -- we also want to make it clear we're not disputing the authenticity and we understand that the Defence position is that it may have sufficient weight to be used for impeachment purposes, and that's then -- and that -- that's about the best we can say about the document at the moment. I don't know if Mr. Robinson wants to add something, but I -- I don't want to create -- I don't want to be misunderstood, as has occurred once in the past, that the Prosecution is disputing the position that either party is entitled to attempt to impeach a witness with a document that purports to do so, and there's no question about the authenticity of this document in that sense. However, there are a variety of other circumstances, some of which were identified by the witness, and some of which appear on the face of document that lend this document such little weight that we don't think its admission is of any assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I indicated, the Chamber received the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1842, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Two more documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three, Your Excellency, very important documents, very brief, but very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Karadzic, you should have put that question for your first available moment in your cross-examination. Do not leave that important questions at the last moment. That will not be admitted later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my notion of dramaturgical effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you didn't dabble in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that it was taken against you because it was said how come you were in the JNA but not in the BiH Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 06490 -- 1D04629. Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic writes in this document about -- I don't know if there is a translation. There should be a translation. He says: [As read] "It may be stated that Dr. Mirza Mujadzic harms our army and the entire people with its destructive behaviour and that he could not perform any of command functions either in the government or the -- in the BiH Army. We will continue gathering evidence on the activities of Dr. Mirza Mujadzic." In other words, you made some requests on the army and then Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic wrote the army staff asking not to approve that. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the Supreme Command issued a document, 0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The -- the document was dated 24th December 1992, and they requested information about your conduct and behaviour. The response was that your conduct was of such nature that you shouldn't be counted with -- either within the army or the government. Can we now look --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What conduct do you have in mind? Could you please be more specific? Is there a more specific document or is this just purely a political statement on the part of Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic? This is more of a political statement than a statement of fact. Enver Hadzihasanovic was a member of the BiH Army just for a brief time and then he fled abroad. His credibility is really very questionable. There's information that, actually, he worked against the BH Army, and it is really a question, what is it that you're trying to present as a fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to present anything. I'm just putting to you what he sent to the Supreme Staff of -- of -- of the BH Army. At that time he was the commander of the 3rd Corps when he wrote that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at 65 ter 20594. Let's see what Sefer Halilovic, the then Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is the document to which Hadzihasanovic responded. It says here Mirza Mujadzic is currently somewhere in the area of Travnik and has also been visiting Zenica. He has been proposed for the position of the president of Banja Luka district based in Travnik or Zenica. We were informed by the military security service that he collaborated with the Chetniks and handed over to them the weapons bought by the people who organised themselves with the Patriotic League and so on and so forth. And now he is requesting a reply and the reply did come. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document, and this is precisely the proof that within the structures of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the Bosniak side there were still a lot of those who co-operated with the counter-intelligence service of the JNA. We had a lot of people, in other words, who worked against us and collaborated with the army and who presented information which was not credible. The fact is, Mr. Karadzic, that after this, I was vetted and that these allegations were proven as inaccurate, that I did become the president of the district and that I remained working as an MP until the end of my office and that after that I held very important positions on the international level, that I was a member of a number of international delegations and all of that speaks volumes about my credibility. I was a member of the delegation that was invited by the CDU party on Malta on 1994 and this speaks volumes about my credibility, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm only dealing with the documents that BiH generals drafted and exchanged with your regard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted and then I will call up my last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering the previous document from ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, both the letter and the answer, i.e., the question and the answer or, rather, the initial letter and the response to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark the previous document for identification and we'll admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 1D4629 will be MFI D1843 and 65 ter 20594 will be Exhibit D1844.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And your last question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you propose to the BiH Army the final showdown with Serbs and the expulsion of the Serbs from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. It never even occurred to me to do something of that sort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D4669.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at your document. These are my of the condition in the BiH Army and proposals of concrete measures. There should be a translation. You present yourself here as member of the Executive Board of the SDA of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not as the chief of a regional body. And now look at -- this is not the right document. 1D4469. No. Actually, this is the right document, but we need the translation. And it says that in September on the 13th of September after Operation Storm was over in Croatia you proposed what needed to be done and in conclusion you say: [As read] "I believe that in this way in a relatively short period of time and in view of the fact that the situation in -- among the enemy ranks is deteriorating by the day, we could embark on a Bosnian storm." You were already familiar with Operation Storm because that had taken place in early August; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but I don't know where you find the element where I proposed the expulsion and ethnical cleansing of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, when you mention a Bosnian storm, you will agree that Storm, it was an operation in which a lot of Serbs disappeared and were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is a Bosnian storm. It doesn't imply the expulsion of Serbs. And this was, indeed, done. Mr. Dudakovic and Mr. Alagic did do the storm in a very correct way, with full respect of the Geneva Conventions. Mr. Karadzic, we defended our state. If we had not defended it, we would not have saved it. We did prepare for defence if we hadn't we would not have saved Bosnia. What is questionable here is how the two sides conducted each other and whether Geneva Conventions were respected. We did that and this is why you're here, Mr. Karadzic, because in your case you did not respect the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Mujadzic, do you agree you could have achieved all of that, if not more, without a war. Everything was better than the Dayton Accords. Everything could have been done without the war.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I couldn't agree more. None of us wanted a war. We all tried to avoid a war, because we knew that we would have -- we would suffer the most if there was a war. That's why we tried to avoid it at all cost. Everything we did, all of our activities, both political and others, were in order to avoid a war, and we did prepare ourselves, but for possible defence, because we knew that the course of events in Slovenia and Croatia could take us and lead us to a similar situation, and this is the long and the short of it, Mr. Karadzic, and I agree with you that all of us wanted to avoid the war -- the war. We should have only been so lucky to have avoided it and if we had, we would have both fared better. You would have probably remained in a high position in Bosnia and Herzegovina if we could have avoided the war and if we could have reached a political agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to correct the transcript. It was not recorded that a storm was a military operation in Croatia that resulted in the expulsion of Serbs from the Serbian Krajina. Dr. Mujadzic, what I am concerned with here is this metaphor Bosnian storm which prompted me to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I could provide just one more comment. Mr. Karadzic, in this document when I referred to a Bosnian storm, what I had in mind was an efficient operation, an efficient offensive. I did not have in mind the effects of the Croatian Storm as a result of which Serbs had left the area where Storm had taken place. Please do not confuse the two terms and do not confuse the implications that had arisen from the Croatian Storm and think that they would have arisen from the Bosnian storm. This was proven by practice because the Bosnian storm did happen. You know that the area from Kupres down to Grahovo, Mrkonjic Grad, Kljuc, and Sanski Most and Bosanski Petrovac was indeed liberated through that operation but the Geneva Conventions were observed and that the Bosnian storm took into account all the aspects of the Geneva Conventions and that it did not result in the same effects as the Croatian Storm. So you cannot put the two terms together and talk about them in -- in the same breath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, but the fact is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic. Your time is up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, we're talking about credibility and discordant statements. We have not touched upon anything. There is so much that we should still discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unacceptable. You asked for 15 minutes more, although there was some mess with respect to e-court, we ended up allowing you almost 40 minutes. Your excuse that there still remains -- there still remains an important question at the last moment will not be accepted in the future. As emphasised many times you have to prioritise your questions and focus on important questions first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Before we move to the redirect, I would like to make a move for motion for reconsideration by the Trial Chamber of the time that it allotted for cross-examination and for certification to appeal the Trial Chamber's decision on the amount of time that Dr. Karadzic had to cross-examine this witness. I know that reconsideration requires some new information and I'm hoping that -- but now that you've seen the cross-examination, you see that Dr. Karadzic was focused, there was very little intervention by the Prosecution or the Chamber concerning the relevance of what he was asking and he still has many more topics to cover. It's hard to ask for reconsideration when we don't really understand the reason for the decision in the first place. And I have to tell you that as Dr. Karadzic's legal advisor I tried to advise him and explain to him why the Chamber makes the decisions, and sometimes how I think the Chamber will rule, and I simply don't understand how a witness who testified for eight hours on direct examination, in a case that's now been admitted as the equivalent of direct examination in this case, can be cross-examined for let's say three hours, unless, and I'm only speculating perhaps you count the cross-examination as -- in the Stakic case against Dr. Karadzic's time, in which case, again, we would ask that that be thrown out of the 92 ter and it's useless to us. That cross-examination resulted in a Trial Chamber sentencing Dr. Stakic for life, so it obviously wasn't very effective and it's not in Dr. Karadzic's interest, or I don't think the Trial Chamber's to simply do a rerun of the Stakic case here. So we simply don't understand why the Trial Chamber would think that this proportion of eight and a half hours of direct examination and three hours of cross-examination is in any way commensurate with a fair trial and I cite the Chamber to the Oric decision by the Appeal Chamber on the 20th of July, 2005, entitled Interlocutory decision on the length of the defence case. And in that case the Defence was restricted in the length of the case that they were allowed to put on and the Trial Chamber decided that the Defence would be restricted in the amount of time it would have for its case. And the Appeals Chamber reversed that and they said that although the time doesn't have to be equal that there has to be some rational proportionality to it. And you if apply that principle to this situation, we don't believe that you've demonstrated any rational proportionality, nor have you in fact given any reasoned decision. We know the factors that you use to determine the time for cross-examination but you've never explained to us how those factors apply in this case and how you arrived at such a disproportionate amount of cross-examination. So we think that this issue is one that affects the fairness of the trial, the expeditiousness of the trial, and one which has recurred in the past and is likely to recur in the future. And as a result, an immediate intervention by the Appeals Chamber would materially advance the procedure, because if it turns out you're wrong, then it would be very difficult after -- for the Appeals Chamber to have to rehear witnesses or somehow figure out what was missed by the error in not allowing Dr. Karadzic enough time for his cross-examination. I think for most of the trial we've had an exemplary procedure in which you've tried to give Dr. Karadzic a fair trial, and I think that it's now in -- with the previous witness, KDZ-490, and again with this particular witness, that it's broken down and the rulings of the Trial Chamber have, in fact, denied him a fair trial. So I'd ask you to reconsider your ruling, and if not, to allow to us appeal to the trial -- to the Appeals Chamber so that we can get a definitive ruling from them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from the Prosecution. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just give me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, could you explain again to us how the two prongs of the Rules are met for the purpose of the certification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to the first prong, this substantially affects the fairness of the trial because Dr. Karadzic is not being allowed to elicit information that the Trial Chamber needs to evaluate both the credibility of the witness and the substance of his testimony, to test the substance of the direct examination as well as to put to him matters which can be helpful to his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you move to the second prong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: To the second prong, it's an issue that has happened in the past and is likely to recur. We still have, maybe, over 50 witnesses and the Trial Chamber appears to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But your appeal is with respect to this specific witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is with respect to this specific witness but it would also have an impact on how the Trial Chamber is allowed to make decisions on future witnesses because we're saying that you have not properly applied the proportionality principle so that Dr. Karadzic is given a sufficient amount of time. So if we're found to be correct and the Appeals Chamber sets out the fact that there has to be greater proportionality between the direct examination and the cross-examination, then I would hope that you would give him more time in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What you are not happy with is the amount of time, not the -- the factors for consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult, because you've never told us how you arrive at the two and a half or now three hours. So it's difficult to make an argument against the particular way in which you've applied the factors, but the fact -- the factors that you've given us we don't have any dispute with those factors, it's how they've been applied in this case and we think that, somehow, whatever you did to arrive at the figure of two and a half hours versus eight hours of direct is -- that an error has been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Tieger will respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first, Mr. President, although I'm pleased to respond, I just want to request, again, that when the Defence anticipates that it will be making submissions, we consider it a matter of both collegiality and efficiency that it alert the Prosecution to the fact that such submissions will be made so that our response can be as considered and informed as possible. Let me just quickly address a couple of factors that can't possibly considered comprehensive. I think the Court alluded to the fact that -- or Mr. Robinson alluded to the fact that reconsideration is generally made in light of new facts. I don't believe there has been a showing that such new facts exist here. With respect to certification, I think the Court has focused quite clearly on one of the flaws in that submission, and that is the fact that the -- the issue here is a dispute by the Defence about the time allotted for this particular witness rather than some broader principle. Indeed, the Defence noted that in virtually all of the previous cases, the allocation of time and therefore the underlying principles worked fine and there was no dispute about the principles involved or their application. This is a one-off focus that doesn't implicate the rules for a certification, and I think the Court made that point. Finally, I'd -- I'd simply note some of the underlying factual flaws in the argument. Let me, as an example, use the notion that to the extent the Court wishes to consider the cross-examination contained within the amalgamated statement as -- in its allocation of time and the Defence's rejection of that because of the verdict in Stakic, there's clearly an apples and oranges analysis being undertaken there. The cross-examination may have been as effective as possible under the circumstances. The Court can certainly make that determination based on its experience and professional assessment. That would not have gained, say, the vast amount of evidence against Dr. Stakic or indeed the -- the accuracy of this witness's testimony and the extent to which it could be undercut with the best of cross-examination efforts. So that's an extremely unfair and inaccurate guideline for the use of the cross-examination, and on a variety of bases I think the Defence motion fails.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break now and give our ruling after the break. We'll break half an hour, for half an hour, and resume at 11.00, but if there's to be a delay, the parties will be informed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this, please. Could I propose this for admittance, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1845, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at 5 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay. There was some additional matters for the Chamber in addition to this matter. The Chamber refers to the accused's request for reconsideration and in the alternative for certification to appeal the Chamber's decision on the time allocated to the accused for cross-examination of Witness Mujadzic. First, the Chamber notes that the time was allocated in accordance with the careful consideration of the factors which have been enumerated on numerous occasions. The Chamber then granted the accused's request for a 15-minute extension and later extended that time by a further 25 minutes. Under those circumstances, the Chamber does not consider it in the interest of justice to further reconsider its decision with respect to this witness. Furthermore, the Chamber notes that Mr. Karadzic spent substantive time on issues the Chamber considered to be of peripheral relevance. In addition, considering the submissions the parties with respect to certification of the decision on the time granted for Mujadzic, the Chamber is not satisfied that an immediate resolution of this issue by the Appeals Chamber would materially advance the proceedings at this stage in light of the approach taken by the Chamber in assessing time allocated for cross-examination and the flexibility adopted when the accused shows good cause for an extension of time. That's the ruling, and I wonder whether the Prosecution has re-examination. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, earlier today at transcript page 7 you were giving the percentages of the population in Prijedor, and you said that according to the 1981 census, there were 43 per cent Serbs and 38 per cent Bosniak, and in 1991, that was reversed, 44 per cent Bosniak and what is written in the transcript is 45 per cent Serbs. Is that what you said in relation to the percentage of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said 42.5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. And secondly, if I could call up Defence Exhibit D1842. That was document that was put to you today by Mr. Karadzic at transcript pages 24 and 25. You disputed matters that were put to you by Mr. Karadzic, but I want to -- you to look at another portion of this document. And for Mr. Registrar, it's at the bottom of page 2 in B/C/S and the middle of page 3 in English. Dr. Mujadzic, can you just read the text in -- that's there in relation to the incident at the Hambarine check-point on the 22nd of May, 1992, and then I have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, but I cannot find in the portion that I have before me any description of the incident at Hambarine. Perhaps that is in another part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of page 2 in the B/C/S, the last two lines on that page, and then the top of page 3 of the B/C/S. And in English it's page 3, going over a little way onto page 4 of this six-page document.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here in the last two lines it says on top of everything --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. If you can just review that paragraph, and then I have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the portion where it says: [As read] "As well as all this, on 22nd May, 1992, Mirsad Mujadzic, his brother Emir and his uncles Husein and Esef Crnkic plotted in Crnkic's house the set-up of a check-point in Hambarinsko Polje. They killed two Serb soldiers who had responded to the call-up and seriously wounded three other, one of whom succumbed to his injuries. On that occasion, Milojica --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I meant read the paragraph to yourself. Does this -- doings this accurately refer --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, it's my mistake. Does this accurately reflect what happened at the Hambarine check-point on the 22nd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This does not correspond to the facts at all. I personally never made any decision, any personal decision, that any check-point should be set up, that check-point, nor it did Mr. Crnkic, Esef, or Mr. Husein Crnkic take part in that, nor did my brother, as a matter of fact. And post festum, after the incident itself, when I heard the shooting, I arrived at the check-point and I found there the situation as I described it in detail in the Stakic evidence, but if you want me to, I can repeat my evidence from that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is that you applied medical assistance to the wounded and called an ambulance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I administered medical assistance as best as I could, and I asked that an ambulance be sent, that they urgently be called from the only phone that was available at the time at the local commune there so that the injured could be assisted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what happened to your two uncles, Husein Crnkic and Esef Crnkic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of them died after they were tortured and beaten up in Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, just one thing that I want to point out. I never even touched upon this incident of Hambarine, the incident that in fact triggered the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The accused wanted this document in. He sought its admission. He got it admitted, and I have a right to re-examine on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means. Yes, Ms. Sutherland. That concludes your evidence, Dr. Mujadzic. On behalf of my colleagues and the Tribunal as a whole, would I like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for everything, and I'm happy that I had the honour to come here and testify about these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a matter in relation to yesterday. I want to correct the time-codes that I provided to you in relation to the 65 ter exhibit 40478A, which is now Exhibit P03707. The correct time-code is 00:09:00 to 00:09:12. I also omitted yesterday to advise Your Honour that there was a 65 ter document that was missed in the Rule 92 ter notification, and that is 65 ter number 17373. It's a decision on the annexation to the autonomous region of Krajina dated the 17th of January, 1992. It's an associated exhibit which was discussed at transcript page 3640 to 3641, and belatedly I would ask that this also be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't have any objection but would I like to look at the transcript and the exhibit, but in principle I don't think there would be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, I forgot to mention yesterday that the name was spelt incorrectly in the 65 ter number 20584 which is now Exhibit P03705. It should be Srdjo Srdic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will you come back to us with respect to 17373, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I can do that after the next recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll wait then. Before we bring in -- yes, Ms. Sutherland? Do you have other submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was going to call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to bring you up-to-date on one other matter. You asked me to look into the order in which the pages are assembled in Exhibit D1831 and you were correct that there were some disorder to that submission and we're in the process of rectifying that and submitting the document for translation because the translation didn't match the B/C/S, so we're working on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we bring in the next witness, the Chamber is going to issue two oral rulings. The Chamber refers to the objection raised by the Prosecution on 5th of October, 2011, to the admission of 1D4439 on transcript pages 19975 to 19976, which was marked for identification as D1748 on transcript page 19979 on the grounds, inter alia, that it appeared to be a compilation of third-party statements. The Chamber required an English translation to be able to make -- make a final determination of whether that document should be admitted. The English translation of the document has now been uploaded, and having reviewed the document, it is clear to the Chamber that it purports to be a report drafted by personnel in the Kljuc SJB discussing their findings after interrogating several prisoners and is not a "compilation of statements," as was suggested by the Prosecution when the issue of its admission was discussed. Under those circumstances, the Chamber is of the view that the Prosecution's objection to its admission has no basis, and MFI D1748 will be admitted in full. The Chamber also refers to the accused's objection to the admission of three documents sought to be tendered through Witness Atif Dzafic on 30th of September, 2011, given the questions raised about their authenticity. The documents objected to were 65 ter 848, which was marked for identification as Exhibit P3514; 65 ter 849, which was marked for identification as Exhibit P3490; and 65 ter 849A, which was marked for identification as P3511. The Chamber has reviewed the documents in question. With respect to MFI Exhibit P3514, the Chamber notes that the authenticity of 65 ter number 23482, already admitted as Exhibit P3572, was not challenged. Exhibit P3572 refers to the decision of the War Presidency of Kljuc, which is found in MFI Exhibit P3514. Under these circumstances, the Chamber is of the view that there are sufficient indicators of authenticity when read in light of P3572 for MFI P3514 to be fully admitted.
