The Chamber is also satisfied that MFI P3511 has sufficient indicia of authenticity to be admitted in full. In contrast, MFI P3490 does not appear to have a protocol number nor does it appear to have a signature. Given that MFI 3490 appears to be a copy of MFI P3511, save the protocol number, the Chamber is of the view that MFI 3490 need not be admitted. Bear with me a minute. We'll break for five minutes for technical reasons for the purpose of bringing in the next witness. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness after the next witness -- actually, the two witnesses after the next witness are the subject of our motions concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are going to give the ruling after that five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Great. Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.57 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before the witness takes solemn declaration, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling. Please be seated, Mr. Witness. In relation to the accused's motion for interviews of two Prosecution witnesses of 31st October 2011, the Chamber has decided that it is competent to rule on the motion in the interests of justice given the urgency of the matter. Turning to the merits of the motion, the Chamber has reviewed the motion and the submissions of the Registry, as well as the protocol for contact -- sorry, for contact between a self-represented accused and witnesses. The Chamber has assessed the Registry's decision not to allow in-person interviews for two witnesses in light of the standard for judicial review of administrative decisions. Given that the validity of the protocol was not challenged by the accused, the Chamber confined its assessment to whether the Registry's decision was not unreasonable in applying the protocol. Given the absence of material which would require visual contact between the two witnesses in question and the accused, the Chamber is of the view that the Registry was not unreasonable in deciding that the accused had not adequately shown good cause for meeting these witnesses in person. As a matter of fact, the Chamber observes that witnesses may be interviewed prior to their testimonies by one of the accused's legal associates or by the accused himself over telephone. In relation to the accused's alternative request that the Prosecution proofs its witnesses over the telephone in order to ensure equality of arms, the Chamber recalls that equality of arms does not equate to equality of means and resources. Accordingly, the Chamber sees no merit in this request. For all of the above reasons the motion is denied. Thank you for your indulgence and patience, Mr. Witness. Could you please stand and take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, you will be testifying today with the benefit of pseudonym and image distortion. This means that there will be no reference to your real name or information which might reveal your identity to the public media -- public or media. The audio-visual record of your testimony which is to be broadcast to the public will have a distorted image like this to ensure that your identity is protected and the transcript, while available to the public, will always refer to your pseudonym. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could 65 ter 9020 be displayed for the witness but not broadcast, please. This is the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, do you see on the screen in front of you your name and pseudonym number in this case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that for admission under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3715 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, as we discussed, part of your evidence in this case is -- will be submitted in writing, and we first need to deal with the formalities with that submission. You provided a statement to representatives of the Prosecutor of ICTY and testified as a protected witness in the Stanisic and Zupljanin trial on the 21st and 22nd of January, 2010. You've subsequently had an opportunity to review the audio recordings of that testimony; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And can you confirm that accurately recorded the statements that you made at that time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: I confirm that that is identical to what I said in the Stanisic Zupljanin trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you were asked about the matters you testified to in the Stanisic Zupljanin case would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber and that is even if you couldn't formulate everything in the same words, the essence of your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: That's right. Basically they would be the same because I cannot think in any other way or give answers in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter number 2 -- 22164, which is the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there will also need to be a redacted version because there were certain things said in open session which were then subsequently redacted and so we will -- which will -- would go to revealing his identity. So we will ensure that there's a redacted public version available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Confidential version will be Exhibit P3516, under seal, and public redacted version will be Exhibit P3517, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with Your Honours' leave I now read a summary of the witness's written evidence. The witness testified to the personnel and structure of the Manjaca camp, and this is scheduled detention facility C 1.2. He testified that Bozidar Popovic was appointed camp commander around 15 June, 1992, and that the Manjaca camp was guarded by military and civilian police. He testified to the conditions and treatment of detainees at the Manjaca camp and described procedures followed from the arrival of new detainees to their release to the camp, including the processing of the detainees which included detainees older than 60 years of age and younger than 18 years of age. The witness testified that 95 per cent of the detainees were Muslims. In addition, he provided evidence that non-Serb detainees were brought to the Manjaca camp by the RS MUP although they had no weapons and had taken no part in armed rebellion. The witness testified about the transport of the detainees to the Manjaca camp by personnel from the RS MUP and, in particular, he testified that on the 7th of July, 1992, 24 detainees from Sanski Most municipality died on their way to Manjaca because of extremely inhumane and unprofessional conduct of the civilian authorities, especially the Sanski Most police. The witness testified that he was personally astounded because people were packed like sardines in a truck covered with tarpaulin and some people were already old or had health problems that contributed to their death. The witness testified that only living were admitted to the Manjaca camp while the bodies of the deceased were returned on the same truck, probably to Sanski Most. And this is scheduled incident B 1.2. In addition, the witness testified to the killing of a number of men in front of the Manjaca camp upon their arrival from the Omarska camp on the 6th of August, 1992, and this is scheduled incident B 1.3. He testified that detainees from Omarska were brought to Manjaca camp by members of the Prijedor police. The witness also gave evidence in relation to the killing of Esad Bender and Omer Filipovic at the Manjaca camp. This is scheduled incident B 1.4. The witness testified that the perpetrators were immediately identified and an investigating magistrate asked for an investigation to be launched. The witness testified that the perpetrators were tried in 2007. That completes the summary of the witness's written evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, as we discussed, I wish to show you a limited number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 05557 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the 1 -- 1st Krajina Corps' commander approval dated the 3rd of August, 1992, for a visit by the international committee and a team of reporters to the detention camps in Manjaca, Trnopolje, Omarska, and Prijedor. It states that all measures are to be taken to make conditions in these camps satisfactory. This implies order, cleanliness, functional, medical care for the detainees, et cetera. Is this consistent with what happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I cannot see this properly, and maybe it could be enlarged if necessary. I remember that this was the document that was sent to all camps, and it is Manjaca that is of relevance to me. What was supposed to be done was what is spelled out in this order. So, yes, it is this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender at that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit -- as Exhibit P3718 and just to correct the record, Your Honours the two statements will be 3716 under seal and 3717 as a public redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you testified at transcript page 5307 in the Stanisic Zupljanin case that detainees were transferred from Omarska to Manjaca around the 6th of August, 1992, that 1.460 prisoners of war were brought from Omarska to Manjaca. And you were shown a report of the 1st Krajina Corps report and that is our 65 ter number 04208, dated the 7th of August, which mentions that 1.460 were brought from Omarska to Manjaca, and you were asked if the Omarska camp was -- this was after the Omarska camp was closed and you said yes. My question is: Did further detainees come from Omarska to Manjaca after the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I can remember, no, not exactly from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document states that deaths occurred during the transport. If we could go into private session for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, at transcript page 5310, you testified about Vojo Kupresanin's visit to the Manjaca camp. What was the result of -- of that visit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: I don't know Vojo Kupresanin at all. I've never met him. I've never seen him. However, through my superiors -- actually, I was not in camp on that day for some good reason, I assume. I was not present during that visit. However, on the basis of my superior's report after the visit and also on the basis of what he said to me, I realized that Kupresanin had held a brief meeting in camp with all the inmates, as far as this could be heard, and that he promised them that over 70 per cent of them would soon be released. So in a way he brought anxiety among the inmates, and he made things more difficult to us, if I can put it that way, because the inmates were anxious, and they were waiting for these expectations to be met. However, these were false promises, as it were. So that is what happened during that visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 05634 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: I've never seen this document. Actually, I never saw it over there in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did -- did you review this document the other day since your arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I got to see it here, but as I've said, I did not see it in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And this is a document dated the 1st of October, 1992, from Vojo Kupresanin, signing himself as president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and it's to the Presidency of Republika Srpska, requesting the abolition or pardon for Muslim prisoners kept at Manjaca. Do you --

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Sorry, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you have any comment to make on -- on -- on this document, on the date of the document and the request for pardon of certain Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Well, what can I say? The 1st of October. In a way this is a request that was late. I cannot make a comparison here if I look at these persons listed here, whether they were included in that list of persons who were sent to Geneva for medical treatment. I simply cannot say. I cannot say how come those people are on this list. President Kupresanin is sending this and I don't know why. This is sent to the President of Republika Srpska. So there are very few comments that I can make except for the following: Even if this was the case, it is already the 1st of October, so that is quite late for any kind of pardon or release and why was there a release in the first place or a pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3722, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 05775.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a report written from the Manjaca camp, a daily report dated the 8th of August, 1992, and if we could go to the signature page, please. The second page. We can see that this is a report written by Radomir Radinkovic. On page 2 of the document it mentions -- I asked you a moment ago about the visit of Mr. Kupresanin to the Omarska camp -- sorry, to the Manjaca camp, and it states in this document that the Manjaca camp was also visited by Mr. Kupresanin and his place took visit -- his visit took place on this day. The visit was carried out as per the order of Radovan Karadzic, the president of the Serb Republic of BiH in order to inform the president himself as well as the Assembly. Does this reflect the visit by Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This is a detailed report on that particular visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3724, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 11033 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you testified at transcript page 5316 about the first group of prisoners being released to third countries on the 14th of November, 1992. We can see in front of us this ICRC communication to the press, number 92 of 32. And it states there: [As read] "About 3.600 detained in Manjaca camp have been regularly visited, registered, protected and assisted by the ICRC since mid-July. And after today's operation, some 2.900 of them still remain in Manjaca where the conditions of detention are getting worse, mainly because of increasingly harsh climatic conditions. And today's operation involves 755 detainees being released to Karlovac." Does this -- is this consistent with what you know to be the case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes. This is their report. The numbers don't tell you. I know that 700 detainees were taken from Manjaca, but I'm not excluding the possibility that some had been in hospital in Banja Luka and were joined to the group and that's why the number is 750, or maybe they were simply wrong, but in any case, that's that. On the 14th of November, the first group of detainees were released, i.e., they were sent to Karlovac from where they were to proceed to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3725, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 23101 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 47-page list of names. Do you -- do you recognise this document as a document that I showed you in the last few days since your arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document that you have shown me, but I also saw it at Manjaca, because the International Committee of the Red Cross after the registration of all the detainees in the camp compiled those lists and gave us a copy of those lists to avoid double registration. For the most part -- part, those lists tallied. This is a collective list compiled with the International Committee of the Red Cross. I recognise it for the BAZ number under which they listed each and every detainee.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say the BAZ number under which they listed each and every detainee, what -- can you clarify that? What -- what do you mean? The BAZ number, the ID reference. Yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes. BAZ, BAZ. Or YUB. I see that most of the numbers are B -- BAZ numbers, and those numbers were assigned to every detainee in every camp in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were particularly -- particularly interested in Manjaca. Those were their numbers. Some -- some of them kept those numbers as a souvenir of their days in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this is the ICRC ID reference number you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's the ICRC ID reference number under which detainees were listed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this list dated 23 -- 23rd of November, 1992, has -- has a number, 2.939 names listed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: I don't have any reason to doubt this because it more or less reflects the situation as it was in Manjaca plus those who were released on the 14th of November. If this was compiled on the 24th of November, as you said, that would be that. The total number of detainees that were ever kept in the camp was 4.403.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3726, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say more or less reflects the situation as it was in Manjaca you mean as of that date the 23rd of -- 23rd of November.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Precisely. On the 23rd of November, this could have been the number of people as we see it in here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 05660 on the screen, please. This is a report -- a daily report written in Manjaca camp and if we could go to the signature page on page 2. And then if we could also show the witness page 3 in B/C/S and in English. Which is an official note compiled at the Batkovic collection centre on the 13th of December, 1992

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this -- does this official note on page 3 where it states that 532 prisoners -- persons were transferred from Manjaca camp to the Batkovic camp --

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was. That was one day before the 14 December, before the second group of detainees was released and sent to Karlovac. There was an exchange, i.e., 532 detainees were transferred from Manjaca to Batkovici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the document it says that the said persons were handed over and then there's a signature and then the -- this is also a signature for the commander of the Batkovic camp confirming that the prisoners were received -- the persons were received.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: This official note was compiled in Batkovic in the camp there. I can see that it was compiled by a certain Djoko Vasiljevic whom I don't know but judging from all of this he compiled the official note to report back to Manjaca and also to -- to his superior that those persons, the 532 detainees had been transferred from Manjaca to Batkovic. This is his report and it was signed by him as well as Pantelija Davidovic [phoen], the person who was in charge for handing the persons over to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3727, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, with respect to the associated exhibits, I just note one thing. This exhibit 65 ter number 5601, which is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I do seek leave to add 65 ter number 23486, which is an associated exhibit which -- associated to the Stanisic Zupljanin transcript but was not on our 65 ter number -- list, exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's no position from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't object, Mr. President, nor do we object to any of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Except for 65 ter 5601 and for those already admitted they will be admitted into evidence and given numbers. Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Could you identify those that should be put under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In the comments column of the Rule 92 ter notification we state whether a document needs to be under seal or not, but we will double-check that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see 65 ter number 5757, which was admitted Exhibit P3724 briefly. Was it -- was the thing that you misspoke about the date, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's not the right document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The document that's on the screen is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems that the wrong document has been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. That's certainly not the one that is referred to. Your Honour, I didn't mention 5757.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, you did, but probably it's a mis -- what number --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The one that I mentioned, the very first one I mentioned was 05557 and that's a 1st Krajina Corps command document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The 5757 was referring to Kupresanin's visit under Mr. Karadzic's order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is 05775, and my apologies if I misspoke with the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. While we're dealing with exhibits I can advise the Chamber that with respect to the exhibits sought to be added with the last witness 65 ter number 17373, we don't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3728, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a query for the interpreters. It's time to take a break for 15 minutes, but instead of taking a break now, how about going till the end, until 1.30 instead of 1.45. THE INTERPRETER. (Microphone not activated) Keep going until 1.30 without a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is agreeable for us to go until 1.30 without a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll do so, thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the videolink interview. I hope this will help us to bring the cross-examination to an end within the given time. I would like to briefly go through today's transcript and then we will move on to documents. On page 51, Ms. Sutherland quoted and said that they were all civilians and that they didn't wear uniforms and so on and so forth. Do you remember where the -- a single detainee at Manjaca had admitted that they had participated in fighting?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Of course I cannot generalise, but the truth is that there were also detainees who had been brought in wearing uniforms from the front lines in small groups, especially in August and September. They had been brought from Derventa, Brod. In other words, there were such men. Don't ask me about any detail, but, yes, I can confirm that there were such men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I may have not put my question precisely enough. Were there people from the Sana valley, Kljuc, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi? Did any of them admit that they had participated in fighting over there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: I -- or, rather, my service at Manjaca could not either practically or theoretically interview all the detainees given their number. However, what we could learn from our direct contacts was that some people had said that they had rifles or pistols for which they had a valid licence. There were people like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you know, don't you, that from the end of May for a week or so there had been fierce fighting going on in Kljuc, Sanski Most, and in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: I arrived on the 15th of June. Before that I was far away from there. I was in Han Pijesak, Pale, Sarajevo, Sokolac, and so on and so forth. Before the 15th of June -- or, rather, before the 5th or 6th of June, I was not there although I was born there. However, my war path meandered from Zagreb to Sarajevo, Pale, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Crna Rijeka and then from Crna Rijeka I was re-assigned to go to Banja Luka where I arrived in Manjaca and that general area. So I can't answer your question based on anything else but media report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, through your communication with your colleagues, did you learn about the fighting that had lasted for approximately a week, for example in Kozarac, Hambarine or perhaps that lasted for two, two and a half weeks? Did you ever learn that there had been fierce fighting going on there in late May and early June?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that from my colleagues. I heard that there had been fierce fighting going on there in Prijedor and around Prijedor, in Kozarac, Kljuc, Hambarine. I don't know who those villages belonged to -- or, rather, to which municipalities, whether they belonged to Sanski Most or to some other municipality. There was fighting there, yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 52, you were shown an order by the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps or somebody from that command according to which you should be prepared for a visit, that you should improve things, because the International Red Cross was about to visit you. Was that something new, or is it the case that it had always been the position of the command to improve things as much as possible?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: From the moment I arrived in Manjaca, which was around the 15th of June, on several occasions I received documents from my superiors regarding the detainees, regarding the compliance with the Geneva Conventions. So that was nothing new. Such documents arrived at my address personally while I was in (redacted) and Sarajevo, and especially at Manjaca. Those were customary reminders, documents that were commonly sent to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So those documents did not need any excuse; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then on page 54, you were shown a request sent to the public security stations to provide some accompanying documents, and you said that the documentation was not updated, that it was not complete, and my conclusion was that perhaps the documents were not professionally done. Do you agree that the documents arrived eventually, sooner or later, updated or not at your request?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Sutherland, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we go into private session very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I thank Madam Prosecutor, who is so careful to protect my identity. Mr. Karadzic, my reply is this: The official correspondence and information from the public security station sometimes arrived with the prisoners themselves, but we intervened because we did not always receive accompanying documents for each and every one of the detainees, and we felt that it was necessary to provide the status of prisoner of war for these people. So we generally requested and our superiors at the corps command then forwarded our request to the security stations, and then they would send people to interview the prisoners of war again in order to compile their statements, or they would bring the statements from the interviews that they had already conducted at the public security station with them when they came. So that's -- it went on and on like that without cease.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the transcript to be completed, but would you please also be mindful of it.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So could it be said, then, that when a smaller group of prisoners was sent or arrived, it was easier to provide accompanying documents for them than when a larger group arrived. Did you notice that there was a pattern there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Well, yes. One could say that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now on page 55, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: (redacted) So does this also prove that there was no cover-up of these cases either, and do you -- can you tell us if you know of any case where there was a cover-up of an incident?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes. This was standard procedure, and we never covered anything up, and as far as I'm concerned especially, my duties within the service in Manjaca, we informed every evening at the end of the day. We reported the security squad of the 1st -- or department of the 1st Corps, and then they would forward on up the chain of command that information to the corps command. So there was no cover-up of any kind, and I didn't do it, and as far as I'm concerned, it never happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, as far as you know, and we've seen the information going from the bottom up, but was there anything coming from the top down, any kind of inappropriate order or permission to act in an illegal or unlawful way?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: I have already said this during my testimony in the Zupljanin and Stanisic case. I've never read any document that would deliberately order the suffering or abuse of people or any kind of inhumane treatment of people. So I've never received any oral or written order or instruction to that effect. I've already said this. Perhaps you -- someone might not like my answer, but I cannot tailor my truth to somebody else's tastes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 56, it was suggested that you very carefully through a sieve, as it were, monitored who was captured, who had been taken prisoner of war, and that perhaps there was -- unless there was someone there who shouldn't be there, and then you would ask for that particular case to be reviewed. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take care of it, Ms. Sutherland. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But am I correct that other than the tragic incident in front of the camp, that over these 150 days there were only five fatalities, two of which were of unnatural causes, whereas three were of natural causes?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: It is true, Mr. Karadzic. All those -- in all those days and of all -- and of the total number of the people who were registered, there were only ten fatalities, two of which were violent deaths, and three were of natural causes. The two violent deaths, which really shocked me, in those cases we did what any other service in the world would do. We discovered the perpetrators. We conducted our investigation, discovered the perpetrators, carried out post-mortems, and provided all documents to the relevant Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So based on those documents that you provided, the perpetrators were later tried and prosecuted; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes. Based on this paperwork these four men were prosecuted and tried, and three of them were sentenced to long sentences. This did happen much later, that is true, but they were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, your constant requests for information in order to understand why somebody was taken prisoner and detained, was this something that was a natural result of the existence of these several layers of authority, because in that case, there would be instances that can actually check on and control other people's work, so did you feel that the reason was that there should be higher-ups who could then check and control what their subordinates were doing and, if necessary, correct their actions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Well, could you please put that question more specifically and tell me what it is you expect me to answer. What is it that you want me to answer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you were very strict, and as I've already said, you used a sieve to carefully consider each and every single case to make sure no-one remained detained without justification. Now, would you agree with me that that is the purpose of having several levels of government so that the higher-ups or the superiors can check the work of their subordinates and make sure that they can correct their mistakes and ensure that everyone is treated in a humane way?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes. I was never a freelancer, as it were. I wasn't free to do whatever I pleased. I was just a person who carried out the orders -- the concepts and the orders that came from the higher commanders. At times, I was perhaps more zealous in my work, perhaps more than another person would be, but I never did anything wilfully. The orders came from my superiors, and at times I was even upset that there was no response of any kind to my reports, whereas you would want to have such a response immediately, in a day or two. Ten days would have been too late for me or was too late for me to wait for a response whether we should and could release the elderly or the infirm, the young, and so on. So there was a certain gap there between what I would have wanted and the reality as it was, but at times there were reactions that I never even learned of at the time. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: duty-bound to inform me as to what steps he had taken, and perhaps I, a little hurriedly, interpreted that as lack of response of any kind, but, well, here now I can correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, am I correct to say that you never received any criticism from the higher commands because you were hard working and zealous, that you were not under any pressure because you were strict and hard working, applied yourself so seriously to the job?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Well, I never received any criticism nor any objection to my overzealousness, but as I've already said, no one from my superior command ever considered that those people should be killed or anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honour, redaction on page -- what's on my LiveNote at page 77, lines 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's being taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, your last question for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 58, my -- Madam Sutherland said that she had shown you a decision on pardon that arrived from the 1st Krajina Corps. Would you agree with me that a pardon comes from the Presidency and the 1st Krajina Corps would just forward it? And would you agree with me that a pardon would come and came as a result of a proposal from the 1st Krajina Corps which had within its competence the prison?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-163
utterances.text: Yes. That was evident from that document, except that we did not really look at the heading. It was an order from the 1st Krajina Corps, but it said, "Pursuant to an order from the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." I believe that's what it was called at the time, and so on and so forth. In other words, the 1st Krajina Corps only conveyed the information that was taken by the Presidency to us at Manjaca in order to to implement it. So that is the chain of command. The Supreme Command, the commanders, the corps, and then lower-level units.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If this was my last question then I'm done for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I just make a note: At LiveNote page 69, Mr. Karadzic said that I said that people were brought to the camp in civilian clothes and he generalised it, and he was quoting to what I had said at page 51, and if Your Honours read what I said at page 51, I said the witness testified that persons that were brought from the RS MUP were wearing civilian clothes. So it was limited and not in the general sense of everyone that was brought was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Mr. Witness, sir, we'll adjourn for today and continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. So in the meantime, while you are giving your testimony, you are not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I will do as I was -- and I've been advised.
